Let the outward face-area vectors of a tetrahedron be
\[
u_1,u_2,u_3,u_4,
\]
where \(|u_i|\) is the corresponding face area. These vectors satisfy
\[
u_1+u_2+u_3+u_4=0.
\]
For any three of them, say \(p,q,r\), the tetrahedron volume \(V\) satisfies
\[
V^2=\frac{2}{9}\,|p\cdot(q\times r)|.
\]

Choose the three face-area vectors with lengths \(1,1,t\), so that the fourth also has length \(t\). Write
\[
|p|=|q|=1,\qquad |r|=t,\qquad |p+q+r|=t.
\]
Let
\[
x=p\cdot q,\qquad y=q\cdot r,\qquad z=r\cdot p.
\]
The condition \(|p+q+r|=t\) gives
\[
x+y+z=-1.
\]
The squared triple product is the Gram determinant
\[
\Delta=
\det\begin{pmatrix}
1&x&z\\
x&1&y\\
z&y&t^2
\end{pmatrix}.
\]
By symmetry in \(p,q\), the maximum occurs when \(y=z\). Put \(y=z=-s\). Then \(x=-1+2s\), and
\[
\Delta=4s(1-s)(t^2-s).
\]
Thus we maximize
\[
s(1-s)(t^2-s).
\]
Its critical point in the admissible interval is
\[
s=\alpha:=\frac{1+t^2-\sqrt{t^4-t^2+1}}{3}.
\]
Therefore
\[
\Delta_{\max}=4\alpha(1-\alpha)(t^2-\alpha).
\]
Since
\[
V^2=\frac{2}{9}\sqrt{\Delta},
\]
the largest possible volume is
\[
\boxed{\frac{2}{3}\left(\alpha(1-\alpha)(t^2-\alpha)\right)^{1/4}},
\qquad
\alpha=\frac{1+t^2-\sqrt{t^4-t^2+1}}{3}.
\]
